parts.title: Hearing and eyesight problems in middle-aged and older adults: a study of how people move between normal thinking, mild thinking problems and dementia, using the Health and Retirement Study
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Background

When people have trouble seeing or hearing, they are more likely to have problems with their thinking, and more likely to develop dementia. But most studies follow people over time and only look at one final outcome, such as whether someone has dementia. That kind of study often cannot tell us which part of the journey is affected. Hearing or eyesight problems might be linked to an early drop in thinking skills, to a slower recovery from those problems, to faster progress toward dementia, or simply to people dying and leaving the study.

Methods

We used data from the Health and Retirement Study, a large survey of older adults in the United States, collected from 2004 to 2022. We used a statistical method called a multistate Markov model. It follows each person as they move between different states over time, and it can handle the fact that people are checked only every few years. We set up four states: normal thinking, mild thinking problems without dementia (called cognitive impairment no dementia, or CIND), dementia, and death.

Our study group included 18,292 people. Our main analysis used 16,083 of them, who had complete information on everything we needed. We sorted people by how they rated their own eyesight and hearing at the start of the study. The four groups were no problems, eyesight problems only, hearing problems only, and problems with both.

Our main analysis took into account age, sex, education, wealth, signs of depression, and the number of long-term illnesses. We also ran extra checks. In some, we used people's eyesight and hearing ratings as they changed over time, or as they were rated in the survey before the one we were studying. In others, we used a method called inverse-probability weighting, which corrects for the fact that people with complete information may differ from those without it. In the last, we took into account more other factors that could affect the results.

Results

Compared with people who had no eyesight or hearing problems, people with eyesight problems only, hearing problems only, or problems with both were more likely to move from normal thinking to mild thinking problems. We measured this with a hazard ratio, which compares how quickly one group moves between states with how quickly a group without problems does. A value above 1 means faster, and a value below 1 means slower. Each value comes with a 95% confidence interval, a range that shows how precise the estimate is.

The hazard ratios for moving from normal thinking to mild problems were 1.18 (95% confidence interval, 1.10–1.27) for eyesight problems only, 1.16 (1.07–1.25) for hearing problems only, and 1.37 (1.26–1.50) for problems with both.

People with eyesight problems only and people with problems with both were also less likely to recover from mild problems back to normal thinking. Their hazard ratios were 0.79 (95% confidence interval, 0.72–0.86) and 0.84 (95% confidence interval, 0.75–0.94).

The links with moving from mild problems to dementia, and with moving to death, were less consistent. Our extra checks, using ratings that changed over time, ratings from the survey before the one studied, inverse-probability weighting, and more factors taken into account, all supported the same pattern for these early moves.

Conclusion

Eyesight and hearing problems, especially problems with both, were most consistently linked to an early drop in thinking skills and to slower recovery. They were not consistently linked to faster progress toward dementia or to moving to death. A model that includes death may help show where eyesight and hearing problems, which might be possible to treat, are connected to the way thinking skills change as people age.

Keywords: thinking skills and ageing, mild thinking problems without dementia, Health and Retirement Study, multistate Markov model, eyesight and hearing problems
parts.introduction_first:
As people live longer, more and more of them develop dementia or have trouble seeing or hearing, and both cause serious problems for public health. The World Health Organization estimated that about 57 million people were living with dementia in 2021, and that nearly 10 million new cases appeared each year. Forecasts from the Global Burden of Disease project, a large international effort to measure health problems around the world, suggest that the number of people living with dementia will rise a great deal by 2050 (GBD 2019 Dementia Forecasting Collaborators, 2022; World Health Organization, 2025).

Problems with the senses are just as common. By 2050, nearly 2.5 billion people are expected to have some degree of hearing loss. At least 2.2 billion people around the world have trouble seeing clearly, either up close or far away. At least 1 billion of these cases could be prevented or are still not being dealt with (World Health Organization, 2019, 2026; GBD 2019 Blindness and Vision Impairment Collaborators and Vision Loss Expert Group of the Global Burden of Disease Study, 2021; GBD 2019 Hearing Loss Collaborators, 2021).

So eyesight and hearing problems are a major reason why older people struggle to do everyday things. They may also be a good place to step in and try to slow the loss of thinking skills and prevent dementia.
parts.conclusion:
Conclusion

We used a model that includes death to follow people through the Health and Retirement Study. It showed that eyesight problems, hearing problems, and problems with both were linked to more people moving from normal thinking to mild thinking problems. Eyesight problems and problems with both were also linked to fewer people recovering from mild problems back to normal thinking. The links with moving to dementia and moving to death were less consistent.

These results suggest that eyesight and hearing problems, especially problems with both, are most strongly linked to thinking skills becoming vulnerable early on and to slower recovery later in life.
parts.introduction_rest:
More and more evidence links hearing loss to a decline in thinking skills, to mild thinking problems, and to dementia. Trouble seeing has also been linked to poorer thinking skills in older adults (Lin et al., 2011; Loughrey et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2022; Livingston et al., 2024). Hearing and eyesight problems often happen together, and having problems with both may carry an especially high risk of dementia (Kuo et al., 2021; Hwang et al., 2022). Studies of older adults in the United States, including the Health and Retirement Study and a related project called HRS-ADAMS, add more evidence. They suggest that eyesight, hearing, and problems with both are linked to a decline in thinking skills, to new mild thinking problems without dementia, to dementia, or to Alzheimer's disease, a common cause of dementia. This was true whether the problems were reported by the people themselves or measured by tests (Maharani et al., 2019; Ge et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024).

However, most studies of eyesight and hearing problems have looked at only one final outcome, such as a decline in thinking skills, new mild thinking problems, or dementia. Studies like these can show whether eyesight or hearing problems predict a later problem with thinking. But they cannot tell us which part of the journey of thinking skills as people age is most affected. Older adults may move back and forth between normal thinking, mild thinking problems, dementia, and death. Some people recover from mild thinking problems. Others move on to dementia, or die before anyone notices dementia.

Death matters a great deal in studies of older people. It is not just a case of someone dropping out of the study. It is a final state that stops the journey, and it competes with the other states. A model that includes death can estimate how eyesight and hearing problems are linked to each separate move between states, while treating death as part of the same process (Putter et al., 2006; Jackson, 2011).

Earlier studies that used this kind of model have looked at education, at patterns of having several long-term illnesses, and at other senses, such as smell. They studied how these relate to moves between states of thinking and to death (Reuser et al., 2011; Robitaille et al., 2018; Knight et al., 2023; Valletta et al., 2023). For example, the SNAC-K study, which followed people from across the population, used a model of moves between normal thinking, mild thinking problems, dementia, and death. It found that a pattern of several illnesses, including eyesight and hearing problems and cancer, was linked to fewer people recovering from mild thinking problems back to normal thinking (Valletta et al., 2023). These studies give us an important example of how to do this kind of research. Yet they have not used the Health and Retirement Study to estimate, separately for eyesight problems, hearing problems, and problems with both, how each is linked to each move between states.

There are good reasons to expect that eyesight and hearing problems might affect different parts of the journey in different ways. Two ideas help explain this. The first is cognitive reserve. This is the brain's ability to keep working even as it changes with age or develops disease (Stern, 2012). Good eyesight and hearing may help people take in information from their surroundings, talk with others, read, find their way around, and make up for other difficulties. Losing these senses may make thinking harder and leave fewer chances to keep up that reserve (Lindenberger and Baltes, 1994; Wayne and Johnsrude, 2015; Whitson et al., 2018). The second idea is sensory deprivation, the idea that losing the senses can leave the brain with less to do. These effects may be easiest to spot before serious brain disease takes over and the person's condition gets worse. That gives us a reason to ask whether eyesight and hearing problems are more strongly linked to an early drop in thinking skills and to recovery than to later moves toward dementia.

We therefore used Health and Retirement Study data from 2004 to 2022 to look at how eyesight problems, hearing problems, and problems with both, measured at the start of the study, were linked to moves between normal thinking, mild thinking problems, dementia, and death. We expected that eyesight and hearing problems, especially problems with both, would be linked to faster decline in thinking skills, slower recovery to a less impaired state, and faster moves to death. We also expected that the size of these links could differ from one move to another. We had decided in advance that the two main moves we wanted to understand were moving from normal thinking to mild thinking problems, and recovering from mild thinking problems back to normal thinking. We treated moving from mild thinking problems to dementia, people being moved back to an earlier state, and moving to death as secondary or extra questions to explore.
parts.methods:
Methods

How we designed the study and where our data came from

We followed the same people over many years, which researchers call a longitudinal cohort study. Our data came from the Health and Retirement Study, a survey that is still going on. It covers adults aged 50 or older in the United States and their spouses, and it is designed to represent the whole country (Sonnega et al., 2014; Health and Retirement Study, 2025). We used waves 7 to 16 of the survey. A wave is one round of the survey, and these waves took place every two years from 2004 to 2022.

We took information about each person's background, health, money and whether they took part in the interview from the RAND HRS Longitudinal File. We then linked this to two other files: one with the survey's measures of eyesight and hearing, and one with the Langa-Weir classification of thinking skills (Crimmins et al., 2011; Langa et al., 2025; RAND Center for the Study of Aging, 2025).

To be included, a person had to be alive at wave 7 and aged 50 or older. At the start, their thinking skills had to be classed as normal thinking, mild thinking problems without dementia (CIND), or dementia. They also had to have eyesight and hearing ratings, sex and education recorded at the start, and a full record of how their state changed over time, which we needed to build our model. This gave us 18,292 people.

Our main analysis took into account several other factors that could affect the results. For this, we used only the 16,083 people who had complete information on all of those factors. We also checked how many people were missing information, and we compared the people in the main analysis with those left out. This let us see whether the two groups were different at the start.

Eyesight and hearing problems

We defined eyesight and hearing problems at the start of the study using how people rated their own eyesight and hearing at wave 7. In 2004, the survey asked people to rate their eyesight while wearing their glasses or other corrective lenses as usual. It also asked them to rate their hearing while using a hearing aid as usual. So what we measured was how well people felt they could see and hear with their usual help, not how sharp their eyesight or hearing was without any help, or the results of a hearing test.

We counted people as having problems if they said their eyesight or hearing was fair or poor, or if they said they were blind or deaf. People who said their eyesight or hearing was excellent, very good or good were counted as having no problems. This gave us four groups that did not overlap: no problems, eyesight problems only, hearing problems only, and problems with both.

We also ran extra checks, called sensitivity analyses, to see whether our results held up when we changed how we measured eyesight and hearing. In some, we used ratings that changed over time. In others, we used ratings from the survey before the one we were studying. In still others, we used a stricter definition of problems, counting only poor eyesight or hearing, blindness, or deafness.

To use ratings that changed over time, we updated each person's eyesight and hearing at every survey wave that had them, using their own ratings for that wave. The model using earlier ratings instead used the ratings from the wave before. These measures show how people's sense of their own eyesight and hearing changed with their usual help. But they cannot tell apart a natural decline from the effects of treatment, people starting to use devices such as glasses or hearing aids, or differences in how the survey was measured.

Thinking skills and death

We defined thinking skills using the Langa-Weir classification. It sorts people in the survey into normal thinking, mild thinking problems without dementia (CIND), or dementia. It uses the survey's questions about thinking skills, and when needed, other information that stands in for them (Crimmins et al., 2011; Langa et al., 2025). We kept only the first record of each person's death and left out all later records. Our main model therefore had four states: normal thinking, mild thinking problems, dementia, and death.

Other factors we took into account

Our main models took into account each person's age, sex, education, wealth, signs of depression, and the number of long-term illnesses at the start of the study. We measured wealth by splitting people into three equal-sized groups, called wealth tertiles. For education, we used the five education groups in the RAND HRS survey.

We measured signs of depression with a standard survey score called the CES-D. We counted long-term illnesses by adding up whether people said they had high blood pressure, diabetes, cancer, lung disease, heart disease, stroke, mental illness, and arthritis.

In one extra check, we also took into account more other factors that could affect the results. These were whether people currently smoked, whether they drank any alcohol, how much moderate or hard exercise they did each week, and whether they regularly went to religious services (at least two or three times a month). We used the last one as a rough stand-in for how socially active people were.

We ran the main model again on the same 16,083 people with complete information that we used for this extra check. This let us separate the effect of taking more factors into account from the effect of using a smaller group of people.

We also checked whether the groups with different eyesight and hearing problems differed at the start. For age, we used a test called one-way analysis of variance, which compares the average age of several groups. For education, we used a test called Pearson's chi-square test, which checks whether the mix of education groups differs between the four eyesight and hearing groups.

The model that follows people between states

We used a type of model called a continuous-time multistate Markov model. It follows each person as they move between states over time, and it can handle the fact that people are checked only every few years. We fitted it to each person's record of how their state changed over time, using a software package for the R programming language called msm (Jackson, 2011).

In our main model, people could move back and forth between normal thinking and mild thinking problems, and between mild thinking problems and dementia. People in any of the three living states could also move to death. Once someone reached death, they stayed there for the rest of the study.

Our main model did not allow people to move straight from normal thinking to dementia. We did this because we see mild thinking problems as a step in between. It also reflects the fact that a change from normal thinking to dementia between two surveys two years apart may include mild problems that nobody noticed. So when we saw a jump from normal thinking to dementia, we treated it as a change that happened sometime during the gap between surveys, not as a sudden medical change. The number of moves we observed in each person's record is given in Supplementary Table S1.

Our main model did allow people to move from dementia back to mild thinking problems. We did this because the survey's classification of thinking skills sometimes went up and down. We treated this move with caution and did not see it as evidence that dementia had truly gone away.

For each of the allowed moves, we estimated a hazard ratio for each eyesight and hearing group, compared with the group with no problems. We also used the model to estimate the chance that a person was in each state, starting from normal thinking and using typical values for the other factors. We then summed these chances up at 5, 10 and 15 years after the start. To make the results easier to understand in medical terms, we also estimated how long people were expected to spend in normal thinking, mild thinking problems, dementia and death. We did this by adding up the chances of being in each state over 5, 10 and 15 years.

Extra checks and further analyses

We ran several extra checks to see whether our main findings about each move held up. We used ratings that changed over time, and ratings from the survey before the one we were studying. We also looked only at people with normal thinking at the start, and left out people who had dementia at the start. We used stricter definitions of eyesight and hearing problems, and we assumed that once someone reached dementia they stayed there. We used more precise death dates, based on the year of death that was available. And we allowed for the possibility of a direct move from normal thinking to dementia.

We also fitted a model using inverse-probability weighting on the 16,083 people with complete information. This let us check whether the people in that group were different from those left out. We also fitted a model that took into account how long people were actually observed in each state, and the extra-check model with more factors described above. Finally, we compared our main model, which assumes the speed of each move stays the same over time, with a model that lets it change over the years. This showed us whether the speed of each move changed as people were followed.

We had planned in advance which moves mattered most for our main conclusions. These were moving from normal thinking to mild thinking problems, and moving from mild thinking problems back to normal thinking. We treated progress toward dementia, moving to death, checks on how the model was set up, and analyses of smaller groups as secondary or exploratory.

Our study was observational, meaning we observed people as they lived their lives rather than assigning treatments. We used a model to study them. So the hazard ratios should be read as links between eyesight and hearing problems and each move, not as proof that one causes the other.

We did not give the people in our main models special weights based on how they were chosen for the survey. This is because we used the model's own calculations of how quickly people move between states. We relied on the way the Health and Retirement Study chose its participants, on taking other factors into account, and on openly discussing this limitation.
parts.results:
Results

Who we studied

Our study group included 18,292 people from the Health and Retirement Study who had at least one survey rating of their thinking skills that we could use in the model. We then kept only people with complete information on everything we needed. That left 16,083 people in our main analysis, the multistate Markov model (Figure 1). The information we were most often missing was people's wealth group (low, middle or high) and their signs of depression. Supplementary Tables S2 and S3 describe the people who were in and out of this complete group.

Figure 1

Who we studied, and how the model works. (a) How people from the Health and Retirement Study were included in our study. The complete group had 16,083 people. (b) How the model follows people over time. It allowed moves between normal thinking and mild thinking problems, between mild problems and dementia, and from each living state to death. Once someone died, they stayed in the death state for the rest of the study.

In the complete group, 10,628 people had no eyesight or hearing problems, 2,104 had eyesight problems only, 2,035 had hearing problems only, and 1,316 had problems with both. The groups differed in age (p < 0.001) and in how much education people had (p < 0.001). The p-value tells us how often a difference this large would turn up by chance alone if the groups were really the same. A value below 0.001 means less than 0.1% of the time. We took age and education into account in every version of the model.

Compared with people who had no problems, people with eyesight or hearing problems were older. They also had more signs of depression and more long-term illnesses (Table 1). People with problems with both were the oldest group on average, and they were the most likely to have thinking problems at the start of the study. At the start, 85.5% of people with no problems had normal thinking. Among people with eyesight problems only, 68.3% did, compared with 75.3% of people with hearing problems only and 59.9% of people with problems with both.

SD (standard deviation) shows how spread out the values are around the average. The depression score (CESD) is a score of how much a person feels depressed.

The main results for each move between states

In our main model, all three groups with eyesight or hearing problems moved from normal thinking to mild thinking problems faster than people with no problems (Figure 2 and Table 2). The hazard ratio was 1.18 (95% confidence interval, 1.10–1.27) for eyesight problems only, 1.16 (1.07–1.25) for hearing problems only, and 1.37 (1.26–1.50) for problems with both.

Figure 2

Main results for each move between states. These forest plots show the hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals for eyesight problems only, hearing problems only, and problems with both, compared with no problems. The estimates come from our main model, which took into account age, sex, education, wealth group, signs of depression, and the number of long-term illnesses. The vertical dashed line marks a hazard ratio of 1, meaning no difference.

Table 2

Main hazard ratios for each move between states, by group at the start of the study.

| Move | Eyesight only | Hearing only | Problems with both |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal thinking → mild thinking problems | 1.18 (1.10–1.27) | 1.16 (1.07–1.25) | 1.37 (1.26–1.50) |
| Normal thinking → death | 1.06 (0.90–1.24) | 0.94 (0.81–1.10) | 1.04 (0.86–1.27) |
| Mild thinking problems → normal thinking | 0.79 (0.72–0.86) | 1.00 (0.91–1.10) | 0.84 (0.75–0.94) |
| Mild thinking problems → dementia | 0.98 (0.88–1.09) | 0.98 (0.87–1.10) | 1.10 (0.97–1.25) |
| Mild thinking problems → death | 1.34 (1.07–1.69) | 1.22 (0.95–1.55) | 0.93 (0.68–1.27) |

Each hazard ratio compares a group with eyesight or hearing problems with people who had no problems. The main model took into account age, sex, education, wealth group, signs of depression, and the number of long-term illnesses.

People with eyesight problems only and people with problems with both were also less likely to recover from mild thinking problems back to normal thinking. The hazard ratio was 0.79 (95% confidence interval, 0.72–0.86) for eyesight problems only and 0.84 (95% confidence interval, 0.75–0.94) for problems with both. Hearing problems only were not linked to this kind of recovery (hazard ratio, 1.00; 95% confidence interval, 0.91–1.10).

The links with moving from mild thinking problems to dementia were less consistent. The hazard ratio was 0.98 (95% confidence interval, 0.88–1.09) for eyesight problems only, 0.98 (95% confidence interval, 0.87–1.10) for hearing problems only, and 1.10 (95% confidence interval, 0.97–1.25) for problems with both.

Across all the moves, people with problems with both were more likely to move from dementia back to mild thinking problems (hazard ratio, 1.25; 95% confidence interval, 1.04–1.49). We included this backward move because survey ratings of thinking skills can go up and down over time. We did not treat it as a real medical reversal of dementia.

The moves to death showed weaker and less consistent links. People with eyesight problems only were more likely to move from mild thinking problems to death (hazard ratio, 1.34; 95% confidence interval, 1.07–1.69). But they were less likely to move from dementia to death (hazard ratio, 0.83; 95% confidence interval, 0.73–0.96). This second result surprised us. No other group showed a clear link with these moves to death. We treated the results about death as less important and interpreted them with care.

Predicted chances of being in each state

We also used the model to predict the chance that a person would be in each state at a given time, starting from normal thinking. These chances differed step by step between the groups with eyesight or hearing problems (Figure 3 and Table 3). At 10 years, the predicted chance of still having normal thinking was 63.7% for people with no problems, 56.3% for eyesight problems only, 61.5% for hearing problems only, and 54.7% for problems with both. The predicted chance of having mild thinking problems was 12.4%, 15.8%, 13.8%, and 17.2% for the same four groups. People with problems with both also had the highest predicted chance of dementia at 10 years (5.7%).

Figure 3

Predicted chances of being in each state, starting from normal thinking. The model predicts the chance of being in normal thinking, mild thinking problems, dementia, or death over time, for people starting from normal thinking in each group at the start of the study. We estimated these chances from our main model, using typical values for the other factors.

At 15 years, the predicted chance of still having normal thinking was 55.5% for people with no problems and 46.5% for people with problems with both. The predicted chance of death at 15 years was 29.6% for people with no problems, 33.5% for eyesight problems only, 30.3% for hearing problems only, and 33.4% for problems with both. Supplementary Figure S1 shows the actual states people were in during the survey years.

We also estimated how many years people were expected to spend in each state, using a version of the model that looks only at the time people were alive. This showed the same pattern, but in years instead of chances (Supplementary Figure S2 and Supplementary Table S4). Over 10 years, people with no problems were expected to spend 7.64 years in normal thinking and 1.14 years with mild thinking problems. Compared with people with no problems, people with eyesight problems only were expected to spend 0.51 fewer years in normal thinking and 0.31 more years with mild problems. For hearing problems only, the differences were 0.19 fewer years in normal thinking and 0.15 more years with mild problems. For problems with both, they were 0.68 fewer years in normal thinking and 0.46 more years with mild problems. Over 15 years, people with problems with both were expected to spend 1.14 fewer years in normal thinking and 0.68 more years with mild thinking problems.

Extra checks

Our extra checks supported the idea that the results for the early moves were stable (Figure 4 and Supplementary Table S5). In one check, we used people's eyesight and hearing ratings as they changed over time. In that check, eyesight problems only, hearing problems only, and problems with both were each linked to faster moves from normal thinking to mild thinking problems. The hazard ratios were 1.25 (95% confidence interval, 1.17–1.34), 1.19 (1.11–1.28), and 1.41 (1.30–1.53). Eyesight problems only and problems with both were also linked to slower recovery from mild problems back to normal thinking (hazard ratios of 0.79, 95% confidence interval, 0.73–0.86, and 0.77, 95% confidence interval, 0.70–0.85).

In another check, we used ratings from the survey before the one we were studying. This gave similar results. Supplementary Figure S3 and Supplementary Tables S6–S8 give more details about these checks and about how eyesight and hearing ratings changed over time.

Figure 4

How well the results for early moves between states held up. These forest plots show hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals for moves from normal thinking to mild thinking problems and from mild problems back to normal thinking. They cover the main model and several extra checks. The checks were: the main model using ratings at the start of the study; ratings that changed over time; ratings from the survey before the one studied; using only people who had normal thinking at the start; leaving out people who had dementia at the start; a stricter definition of eyesight and hearing problems; treating dementia as a state people could not leave; a more precise way of timing deaths; inverse-probability weighting using only people with complete information; the main model fitted again to the larger group; and taking into account more factors: smoking, alcohol use, physical activity, and regular religious participation. Blue circles show eyesight problems only, green squares show hearing problems only, and orange triangles show problems with both. The vertical dashed line marks a hazard ratio of 1.

The results for moving from mild thinking problems to dementia were less consistent across the different versions of the model. Even so, problems with both were linked to faster moves from mild problems to dementia in two checks: the one using ratings that changed over time (hazard ratio, 1.23; 95% confidence interval, 1.10–1.37) and the one using ratings from the survey before the one studied (hazard ratio, 1.27; 95% confidence interval, 1.13–1.42) (Supplementary Figure S4).

In the inverse-probability weighting check, the hazard ratios for moving from normal thinking to mild thinking problems were 1.19, 1.16, and 1.37 for eyesight, hearing, and problems with both. The matching hazard ratios for moving from mild problems back to normal thinking were 0.76, 0.99, and 0.83 (Supplementary Table S6).

In another check, we let people move straight from normal thinking to dementia, without passing through mild problems. The results for the two main early moves did not change much. However, the model's calculations could not be checked properly (it produced a non-positive Hessian, a sign that the model could not be fully trusted). So we used this check only to test the model's structure (Supplementary Table S9). A further check, which split the follow-up time into pieces, suggested that the speed of moves between states changed over time (Supplementary Table S10).

We also explored whether the results differed by age, using a different kind of model (a logistic model) for each move. These results suggested stronger links before age 75. Among people younger than 75, the odds ratios for moving from normal thinking to mild thinking problems were 1.28 for eyesight problems only, 1.17 for hearing problems only, and 1.50 for problems with both. An odds ratio compares the odds of a move between groups, and a value above 1 means higher odds. Among people aged 75 or older, the matching values were 1.08, 1.05, and 1.14, and their confidence intervals included 1, meaning no difference. Eyesight problems only and problems with both were also linked to lower odds of recovering from mild problems back to normal thinking among people younger than 75, but not among people aged 75 or older (Supplementary Table S11). Across groups with different levels of education, problems with both stayed linked to higher odds of moving from normal thinking to mild thinking problems and lower odds of recovering from mild problems. These models were exploratory. The fact that some groups showed statistically significant results and others did not does not, on its own, show that the links really differ by age or education.

In one last check, we took into account more other factors that could affect the results. This included 15,936 people. We added current smoking, alcohol use, physical activity, and regular religious participation to the factors we had already taken into account. The hazard ratios (95% confidence intervals) for moving from normal thinking to mild thinking problems were 1.17 (1.09–1.26), 1.16 (1.08–1.26), and 1.35 (1.23–1.48). The matching hazard ratios (95% confidence intervals) for moving from mild problems back to normal thinking were 0.80 (0.73–0.88), 1.00 (0.91–1.10), and 0.84 (0.76–0.94), for eyesight, hearing, and problems with both. These results were similar to those from the main model using the same people (Supplementary Table S12). This shows that these extra factors did not change the pattern for the early moves much. Religious participation was only a partial stand-in for how socially active people were.

Discussion

We set out to test several ideas about how eyesight and hearing problems relate to the way thinking skills change over time. Our study included people who died during the study, and it followed them through several states. Some of the ideas we planned to test were supported, and some were not.

As we expected, eyesight problems, hearing problems and problems with both were each linked to people moving faster from normal thinking to mild thinking problems. Eyesight problems and problems with both were also linked to people moving more slowly from mild problems back to normal thinking. Problems with both usually showed the strongest link with these early moves. However, we had also expected that people with eyesight or hearing problems would always move faster from mild problems to dementia, and would always be more likely to die. These ideas were not supported. The links were weaker, they varied from one group to another, or they went against what we expected. So the most consistent links we found are about an early drop in thinking skills and about recovery, not about a steady speeding up of every later move.

We also used the model to estimate the chance that a person would be in each state at a given time, such as 10 years after the start. This let us turn the links for each move into actual differences in those chances. Among people who started with normal thinking, those with problems with both had a 9.0 percentage-point lower predicted chance of still having normal thinking at 10 years than people with no eyesight or hearing problems. They also had a 4.8 percentage-point higher predicted chance of having mild thinking problems. A percentage point is a simple difference between two percentages. For example, going from a 50% chance to a 59% chance is a rise of 9 percentage points.

These differences are small for any one person. But they may matter for health care and for public health in older populations. Mild thinking problems are common, they change over time, and they may be easier to prevent than dementia that has already set in.

Our findings fit with earlier research linking eyesight and hearing problems to worse thinking skills. Studies that follow people over time, and studies that combine the results of many earlier studies, have linked hearing loss to a decline in thinking skills, to mild thinking problems, and to dementia (Lin et al., 2011; Loughrey et al., 2018; Livingston et al., 2024). Eyesight problems have also been linked to poorer thinking skills in older adults (Rogers and Langa, 2010; Cao et al., 2022).

In the Health and Retirement Study, Maharani et al. (2019) reported that people who said they had eyesight problems, hearing problems or both were more likely to have a decline in thinking skills, to develop possible mild thinking problems, and to have probable dementia. Li et al. (2024) also found links between eyesight problems, hearing problems and problems with both and the risk of dementia and Alzheimer's disease over 10 years. Other analyses of the Health and Retirement Study, called HRS-ADAMS, used actual hearing and eyesight tests rather than people's own ratings. They also support a link between losing the senses and a decline in thinking skills (Ge et al., 2020). Together, these studies showed that eyesight and hearing problems predict later thinking outcomes. Our study adds to that evidence. It shows that the most consistent links were concentrated in the move from normal thinking to mild problems, and in the move from mild problems back to normal thinking.

Our findings also build on earlier studies that followed people through several states of thinking. Reuser et al. (2011) used a method called a multistate life table, which works out the chance of being in each state over time, to study mild thinking problems, recovery and death. However, they mainly looked at education, body mass index (a measure of weight compared with height) and smoking. Robitaille et al. (2018) studied how education related to moves between states of thinking and to death, using several studies that followed people over time. Knight et al. (2023) added the sense of smell to a model of mild thinking problems, dementia and death.

The study most similar to ours in method was by Valletta et al. (2023). It used data from the Study of Nutrition, Aging and Cognitive Health in KwaZulu-Natal (SNAC-K) to look at patterns of several long-term illnesses together. It modelled normal thinking, mild thinking problems, dementia and death. It found that a pattern of illnesses that included eyesight and hearing problems and cancer was linked to less recovery from mild problems back to normal thinking. Our study adds to this work. In the Health and Retirement Study, it estimates the links for each move separately for eyesight problems, hearing problems and problems with both.

The fact that the links were concentrated in the early moves fits with two ideas. The first is cognitive reserve, the idea that people differ in how much mental "backup" they have, which helps them cope with damage to the brain. The second is sensory deprivation, the idea that losing the senses can leave people with less input from the world around them. Before dementia sets in, good eyesight and hearing may help keep up this backup. They let people communicate, read, get around, find their way and take in information from their surroundings. Losing the senses may make thinking harder and reduce this input (Crimmins et al., 2011; Langa et al., 2025; RAND Center for the Study of Aging, 2025). Cognitive reserve theory offers a further explanation (Stern, 2012).

Other shared causes may also play a part. These include problems with blood vessels, diseases in which brain cells slowly break down, and frailty, a general weakness in older people. Hearing loss has been linked to changes in the brain's nerve cells and in brain size (Lin et al., 2014; Wayne and Johnsrude, 2015; Griffiths et al., 2020). Being cut off from other people and having signs of depression are other possible routes (Mick et al., 2014; Dawes et al., 2015; Kuiper et al., 2015; Yorgason et al., 2022). Once dementia has set in, the damage already done to the brain and the person's wider health may take over how the disease progresses. This could make the role of eyesight and hearing seem smaller. These explanations fit the pattern we saw. But we did not test them directly, and they should not be read as proof that eyesight and hearing problems cause these changes.

We found no link between hearing problems only and recovery from mild problems back to normal thinking, even though we did find links for eyesight problems and for problems with both. This may be because each sense works in its own way, because of errors in how hearing was measured, or because of chance. Eyesight supports reading, finding your way using what you see, getting around and other daily activities that keep the brain active. Actual eyesight tests have been linked to decline in several kinds of thinking skills (Varadaraj et al., 2021). By contrast, people's own ratings of their hearing are not very good at picking up hearing loss measured in a hearing test, especially in adults whose thinking skills are already affected (Kim et al., 2021). This could make the links for hearing problems only look weaker than they really are. Even so, our study is observational, meaning we observed people rather than assigning them to groups. So it cannot show that eyesight matters more than hearing for recovery from thinking problems. The results also varied, and they need to be repeated in other studies.

Problems with both eyesight and hearing may be especially important. When both senses are affected, a person has less ability to make up for one with the other. This may limit how much they can get around, communicate and take part in their surroundings, more than with either problem alone. Earlier studies have linked problems with both to dementia, to serious thinking problems and to faster decline in thinking skills (Maharani et al., 2018, 2019; Ge et al., 2020; Kuo et al., 2021; Fuller-Thomson et al., 2022; Hwang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024). In our study, problems with both showed the largest and most consistent link with moving from normal thinking to mild problems. This pattern stayed the same in several of our extra checks. These findings support treating problems with both as one combined risk when judging the risk of thinking problems, rather than treating eyesight and hearing problems as separate issues.

A key strength of our study is that it included death as a final state that people leave the study through. In studies of older people, death is not just another way of dropping out. It ends any chance of later moves in thinking skills. Ignoring death may give a misleading picture of how dementia develops, especially when the things being studied are also linked to how long people live. Models that follow people through several states can estimate moves between states of thinking and moves from living states to death in the same way (Putter et al., 2006; Jackson, 2011; Reuser et al., 2011; Robitaille et al., 2018; Knight et al., 2023; Valletta et al., 2023). In our analysis, the results about moving to death were not the most stable findings. Their main value was to lower the risk of treating people who died as if they had simply dropped out of the study without telling us anything.

Our extra results, which looked separately at people younger and older than 75, also need to be read with care. Stronger links before age 75 could mean that, at that age, input from the senses and the ability to make up for problems still matter more. In older people, more damage to the brain and more long-term illnesses may take over how thinking skills change. Other explanations are also possible. Some people may have survived longer because of their eyesight and hearing, some people may have been placed in the wrong group, and the results for the older group may be less precise. We did not run formal tests of whether the links differ by age. So the weaker links at age 75 or older should be seen as a starting point for new ideas, not as proof of a clear age cut-off.

The results about moving to death should not be read as showing that eyesight and hearing problems protect people, or that they cause these moves. The hazard ratios for each move only apply to people who are already in mild problems or dementia. The groups with eyesight or hearing problems who reach those states may differ from the others because of earlier moves, how long they survive and the care they receive. Several things may therefore make these estimates unstable or puzzling. There were fewer people with problems with both and fewer people with dementia. Some people may have survived longer because of their eyesight and hearing. Some people may have been placed in the wrong group or state. Other factors that we did not fully take into account may still affect the results. And we made several extra comparisons.

Our inverse-probability weighting analysis corrected for the fact that people with complete information differed from those without it. But it did not correct for people being more likely to reach a state because of their eyesight and hearing, or for factors we did not measure. For these reasons, we see the higher estimate for moving from mild problems to death among people with eyesight problems only, and the lower estimate for moving from dementia to death among people with eyesight problems only, as exploratory.

Our study also has limitations. First, people rated their own eyesight and hearing, using their usual glasses, contact lenses or hearing aids. We did not test their eyesight or hearing with a test of how well they could see or hear. People's own ratings can differ from actual problems, and hearing loss that goes unnoticed may be especially common in people whose thinking skills are already affected (Kim et al., 2021). Our extra checks used ratings that changed over time, or ratings from the survey before the one studied. These captured changes people reported, but they could not tell apart worsening eyesight or hearing from treatment, taking up glasses or hearing aids, or differences in how the survey was measured.

Second, we sorted people into states using the Langa-Weir classification, a system based on survey answers rather than a doctor's diagnosis (Crimmins et al., 2011). People may move back and forth between neighbouring states. So a move from dementia back to mild problems should not be read as a real recovery.

Third, our main model did not estimate a separate direct move from normal thinking to dementia. We also tried a model that included these direct moves, but its results were not stable enough for firm conclusions.

Fourth, the people we left out of the main analysis were older and had more problems with their thinking and their senses. The inverse-probability weighting estimates were similar to the main results. But we cannot rule out that the people left out differed from those included, and we cannot tell from these data whether that would make the results look better or worse.

Fifth, we did not give each person's survey answer the weight it would have in a survey designed to represent the whole population. So our results should be read as links found by our model in the Health and Retirement Study, not as exact figures for the whole population.

Finally, our expanded model took into account smoking, alcohol use, physical activity and regular religious attendance. But religious attendance is only a partial stand-in for how socially active people are, and other factors may still affect the results. We also checked whether the speed of each move stayed the same over time. This check suggested that the speed of each move may change during the study. So our main estimates show the average link for each move over the whole study period.

Overall, our study suggests that eyesight and hearing problems may matter for thinking skills and ageing from before dementia becomes clear. Studies that look only at the final outcome, such as whether someone has dementia, miss part of the picture. Looking at the move from normal thinking to mild problems, and at slower recovery from mild problems, may better show the window in which checking and treating eyesight and hearing could be tested. Recent studies that randomly assigned people to hearing treatments give important clues about whether treating the senses can change how thinking skills change over time. However, the effects may depend on a person's starting risk, when the treatment begins and how long people are followed (Lin et al., 2023). Future studies should combine actual eyesight and hearing tests with information on hearing aids and glasses, and follow people for longer. This would test whether improving eyesight and hearing can change the early moves between states of thinking.
